newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Observers highlight Cameroon poll problems.
newsitem.headline: Observers highlight Cameroon poll problems.

text.p: Cameroon's weekend legislative election, the second since the advent of multi-party politics in 1990, was tarnished by problems and irregularities, international observers say.

But with opposition parties crying foul after Saturday's vote for a new 180-seat national assembly, the observers reserved judgment on whether or not the poll was free and fair. Formal results are not expected for over a week.

"The organisation of these elections leaves a lot to be desired," said Christine Desouches, coordinator of an 18-member observer team from the Francophone group the Agence de Cooperation Culturelle et Technique de la Francophonie.
"We saw ballot boxes that were not empty (before polling). That is fraud," Isaac Nguema, Gabonese president of the Francophone team, told a news conference late on Monday.
But he said that they had only visited 350 of the 16,010 polling stations and added that they wanted to assess what happened elsewhere before making a final judgment.
The capital Yaounde and the rest of the country were reported calm on Tuesday, a public holiday.
With President Paul Biya seeking re-election in October, Nguema called on the authorities to improve voter registration and identification -- a major opposition complaint.

"We recognise the progress that has been made by the government of Cameroon (but) more needs to be done before the next elections," Canadian legislator Jean-Jacques Blais, chairman of the Commonwealth Observer Group, said.

"The holding of multi-party elections... requires skilled planning and administration, as well as the establishment of a viable legal framework," he told a news conference, calling for an independent electoral commission.
The interior ministry runs elections at present.
"There has to be a distancing between the administration and the electoral process, so that there is a perception that those in power cannot influence the electoral process," said Blais.
On Saturday scores of frustrated, angry people told Reuters in Yaounde that their names did not appear on voters' lists and that they had not been issued voter registration cards.
The nation's two main opposition parties, the Social Democratic Front (SDF) and the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP), have both called for results to be scrapped.
Both parties have urged their supporters to be prepared to defend their rights.

The Front's stronghold is the English-speaking North-West Province, a flashpoint in largely French-speaking Cameroon, but it also draws support from Cameroon's main ethnic Bamileke group and the urban poor.

Front leader John Fru Ndi lost narrowly to Biya in the 1992 presidential election, which the opposition says was rigged. The Front polled well during January municipal elections, taking the nation's biggest city, the port of Douala.
Biya took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982. In the 1992 election, his party won 88 seats. It formed an alliance with a smaller party to form a majority.
